title: Eyes, brain, judgement: How WEX thinks about AI in benefits
summary: Explore how AI in employee benefits is improving claims processing, personalizing guidance and building more intuitive, trusted benefits experiences.
body_markdown:
### Share


For years, the benefits industry has worked toward a simple goal: make benefits information easier to access. Put the information online. Build a better mobile experience. Give employees search tools, educational resources and digital account access. Make it possible for people to find answers when they need them.


But access is only the beginning.


Imagine receiving a notification that you have a claim to submit. Or realizing you need to choose a benefits plan. Or discovering that you have money sitting unused in a benefit account. The information may be readily available. Yet the system can still leave you with the same fundamental question: What do I do next?


That gap between information and action is where the next evolution of benefits technology is taking shape. AI has the potential to help people move beyond finding information to understanding what matters to them, what they should do next and when they should do it. The opportunity isn’t simply to make benefits technology more intelligent. It’s to make the experience more useful while preserving the human oversight necessary to earn trust.


## What we build: AI that helps people act


### From answering questions to understanding context


Traditional digital benefits experiences largely follow the same model: a person asks a question, searches for information, reads the answer and then decides what to do. This approach made benefits more accessible, but it still puts much of the cognitive burden on the individual.


An AI-enabled experience can work differently. Instead of simply responding to a question, AI can understand the context around that question. It can connect information across the benefits journey, identify what is relevant and help route someone toward the next best action. In some cases, it can proactively surface information before a person even knows they need it.


This reflects the same philosophy behind WEXly™, WEX’s virtual assistant experience: AI should do more than retrieve information. It should help people understand their unique situation and move forward.


The distinction is important. The value of AI isn’t measured simply by how quickly it can answer a question. It comes from what happens next.


### Make the moments that matter easier


Claims are one of the clearest examples of where this shift from access to action can make a tangible difference. Submitting a claim can require people to gather receipts, enter information, understand eligibility requirements and wait for a decision. For something that should be relatively straightforward, the process can create unnecessary friction.


AI can help at multiple points. It can extract information from receipts and documentation, populate claim fields, validate information in real time and, when appropriate, automatically adjudicate eligible claims.


Just as important, AI can recognize uncertainty.


If a claim doesn’t fit a clear pattern or the system lacks sufficient confidence, the appropriate response isn’t to force an automated decision. It’s to route the case for human review. The point isn’t automation for automation’s sake. It’s removing the routine work that gets in the way while making sure the right expertise is available when complexity requires it.


### Don’t wait for people to know they need help


Benefits often require people to remember something at exactly the right moment.


A claim needs to be submitted. An account has funds available. An enrollment deadline is approaching. A particular benefits decision could have a meaningful impact on someone’s finances.


Historically, the responsibility for remembering those moments has largely fallen on the employee. AI creates an opportunity to change that dynamic.


Rather than expecting people to become experts in their benefits, an AI-powered experience can use real-time signals to surface relevant guidance when it matters. Claims, account information and behavioral data can work together to create a more consistent experience across mobile, web and payments.


The result is a benefits experience that meets people where they are instead of asking them to navigate the system on their own.


### Personalization should improve decisions—not manipulate them


The same principle applies to benefits decision-making. Personalization has long been used to improve digital experiences. But in benefits, the objective should be more meaningful than increasing engagement or driving a particular behavior.


With BeneFITwise Premier, AI can support more intelligent plan guidance and proactive recommendations. The goal is to make information more relevant to an individual’s circumstances so they can make a better-informed decision.


The best use of personalization is to help them understand their options and make decisions that are appropriate for their individual circumstances. And the more consequential the recommendation, the more important it becomes to explain how the system works and how it is governed.


Robert Deshaies, chief operating officer of benefits at WEX, explained:


“For years, the industry focused on access — giving people portals and search bars to figure things out on their own. What good is access, though, if employees don’t actually understand their benefits in the first place?” The real power of AI is context. Through tools like WEX’s BeneFITwise Premier, employees can receive informed recommendations on the most suitable coverage based on their unique needs and current plans. This helps employees overcome decision fatigue during benefits selection, and make confident, data-driven choices that protect their short-term health and long-term financial security.”


# How we govern it: Trust has to be built into the system


### In benefits, the standard for AI is higher


Benefits involve people’s money, personal information, financial security and, in some cases, health-related decisions.


So asking whether AI *can* do something isn’t enough.


We also need to ask:


- Should it do this?
- What data is it using?
- How confident is the system?
- Can a person understand what happened?
- Who is accountable?
- What happens when the system isn’t sure?


For WEX, trust starts with the structure of the system itself.


Our AI operates on rails that WEX owns end to end. That means the technology, the experience and the financial responsibility behind the decision aren’t fragmented across a chain of unrelated technology providers.


That structure also matters because WEX isn’t owned by an insurer. There isn’t a parent insurance product that the system is structurally incentivized to steer people toward.


The distinction matters. It makes the principle of improving decisions, not manipulating them more than an aspiration. It is reflected in how the business and technology are designed.


### Put principles behind the promise


Those structural choices are reinforced by WEX’s six ethical AI principles:


1. Privacy and data governance
2. Technical robustness and safety
3. Non-discrimination and fairness
4. Human agency and oversight
5. Transparency
6. Accountability


These principles aren’t simply a policy checklist. They establish the boundaries within which AI should operate. That’s especially important in benefits, where responsible AI has to translate into decisions that people can understand and trust.


Accountability is a critical part of that equation. When the technology, experience and underlying decision-making are connected, there is a clear place to look when something goes wrong and a clear responsibility to improve it.


### Governance needs more than a policy document


Responsible AI can’t live exclusively in a policy document, an engineering organization or a compliance function. It requires ongoing business, technical, legal and operational judgment.


At WEX, that includes multiple layers of governance, from board and executive oversight to a cross-functional AI Systems and Model Governance Committee and review of high-risk use cases. This process makes sure innovation happens within a framework that recognizes the consequences of getting AI wrong.


This same philosophy extends to how AI systems are built and operated. When an organization owns the experience end to end, accountability doesn’t disappear into a collection of vendors. The people making decisions about how AI is used remain accountable for the outcomes it produces.


### Know when the machine doesn’t know


Perhaps the clearest way to understand this philosophy is through the **“eyes, brain, judgment”** framework.


**Eyes:** AI interprets information such as receipts, documentation and other inputs.


**Brain:** AI applies rules, patterns and context to determine what can be processed.


**Judgment:** When confidence isn’t sufficient, the system recognizes uncertainty and brings a human into the process.


A sophisticated AI system isn’t one that automates every possible decision. It’s one that understands the limits of its confidence and knows when human expertise matters. In this model, human involvement isn’t a failure of automation. It’s an intentional component of the system. AI can handle routine work at scale while directing human judgment toward the cases where experience, nuance or additional context is needed.


And because WEX owns the experience end to end, that escalation can happen within the same system of accountability rather than being passed across a chain of technology providers.


### Trust also means protecting the data behind the experience


The trust equation extends to the data that makes an AI-powered experience possible.


Customer documentation is not used to train foundational AI models. That boundary matters because people should be able to understand not only what AI is doing with their information, but also what it is not doing.


For WEX, protecting customer data isn’t a technical footnote. It is part of the accountability that comes with operating AI in benefits alongside governance, human oversight and a system designed to improve decisions rather than manipulate them.


# How we work: You can’t sell an AI future you don’t operate yourself


### WEX isn’t experimenting from the sidelines


There is another important part of building useful AI: using it yourself.


WEX employees are already working with tools including ChatGPT, Claude, NotebookLM, Gemini and Cursor, alongside internal AI accelerators. WEX isn’t learning about AI solely by developing capabilities for customers. We’re learning what it means to use AI as part of the day-to-day work of an organization.


### Internal adoption creates better products


The feedback loop is straightforward:


Use AI internally, learn where it works, understand where human judgment matters, build better controls, then translate those lessons into customer experiences. This creates a valuable connection between internal adoption and the products WEX builds for customers.


AI shouldn’t be viewed only as a technology purchase. It represents a new way of working and organizations will learn the most by applying it to their own work, understanding its strengths and limitations, and developing the governance and habits necessary to use it responsibly.


# The bigger opportunity for HR and benefits leaders


For HR and benefits leaders, the question shouldn’t simply be:


**Where can we deploy AI?**


A more useful question is:


**Where can AI remove friction, improve decisions and give people more confidence in moments that matter?**


It shifts the focus away from AI as a feature and toward AI as an experience. Away from how sophisticated the underlying model is and toward whether people can actually accomplish something more easily because it is there.


And it creates a more practical way to think about responsible AI.


The right system isn’t necessarily the one that does the most. It’s the one that knows what it should do, knows what it shouldn’t do, makes its role understandable and brings people into the process when human judgment is needed.


# The future of benefits is less about AI—and more about action


The benefits industry has spent years making information more accessible.


The next opportunity is to make that information more actionable.


Imagine a benefits experience that recognizes when someone needs help, makes the next step clear, handles routine work accurately, knows when it isn’t confident, brings in a human when judgment matters and earns trust through the way it is built and governed.


The strongest AI experience may be the one where people barely notice the technology at all. They simply notice that something that used to be confusing is easier. A task that used to take time takes less. A decision that used to feel uncertain feels clearer.


That’s the shift from access to action. Access gave people information. AI can help people turn that information into action.


And ultimately, the success of AI in benefits shouldn’t be measured by how sophisticated the technology is. It should be measured by what it helps people accomplish: making better decisions, taking the right actions and feeling more confident in the outcome.


“When it comes to benefits, you’re dealing with the intersection of people’s health, money, and personal security – some of the most sensitive and important aspects of their lives,” Deshaies said. “That means trust has to be engineered into how benefits are managed and distributed from day one. Our goal at WEX isn’t automation for its own sake. A truly sophisticated system knows the limits of its own confidence, handles the routine work at scale, and intentionally routes complexity to human expertise when real judgment is required.”
